items.title: Impact of postoperative hydrocortisone replacement dose on health-related quality of life and metabolic parameters in patients with cured Cushing's syndrome
items.summary: Single-center RCT (n=42) randomized post-op hypocortisolemic patients after curative Cushing's surgery to 15 mg/day vs. 30 mg/day hydrocortisone for 3 months. No quality-of-life difference between doses, but the 15 mg/day group had better triglycerides, total cholesterol, and HbA1c, with no excess adrenal crises. HPA axis recovery (71% overall) was independent of dose.
items.caveat: n=42, single-center, open-label -- quality of life is self-reported and unblinding could bias that specific outcome. Still directly actionable for a common bedside dosing decision.
items.quiz_question: A 34-year-old woman is 2 weeks post-transsphenoidal surgery for Cushing's disease, biochemically cured, now hypocortisolemic as expected. She asks whether she should take 'more' hydrocortisone to feel better faster. What do you tell her, and what do you monitor either way?
items.quiz_answer: Physiologic replacement (~15 mg/day range) is reasonable and was not worse for quality of life, while giving a better metabolic profile than 30 mg/day. There's no signal that 'more' speeds symptomatic recovery. Regardless of dose: monitor for adrenal insufficiency symptoms (fatigue, nausea, hypotension, hyponatremia), watch for cortisol withdrawal syndrome (myalgia, mood symptoms despite adequate replacement, which can mimic under-replacement), and track HPA axis recovery over time.

items.title: Is Hypercortisolism Treatable? Which Patients Should Be Treated and How-A Practical Guide for Clinicians.
items.summary: Narrative review synthesizing the CATALYST and MOMENTUM studies: confirmed hypercortisolism is rare in unselected T2D/hypertension populations (0.6-3.4%) but reaches roughly 1 in 4 in high-risk subgroups (treatment-resistant T2D, resistant hypertension, adrenal incidentalomas). The review argues against universal screening, recommending the overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test only for multiple/progressive/atypical cardiometabolic features or an incidentaloma.
items.caveat: This is a review restating CATALYST/MOMENTUM data, not new primary evidence -- useful for calibrating your own testing threshold, not a new finding in itself.
items.quiz_question: A patient with well-controlled T2D on one oral agent, normal BMI, and no cardiovascular risk factors or incidentaloma asks about cortisol testing. Per this review's logic, do they meet criteria for hypercortisolism screening?
items.quiz_answer: No -- this patient has none of the flagged features (treatment-resistant T2D, resistant hypertension, adrenal incidentaloma, or multiple/progressive/atypical cardiometabolic findings). The review argues against routine screening in exactly this kind of unselected, well-controlled presentation.

items.title: Hypertension action bundle including training of healthcare professionals to improve the detection of primary aldosteronism
items.summary: French hypertension clinic cohort (2016-2024): primary aldosteronism detection rose from 1.2 to 4.3 per 1,000 consultations alongside staff training on secondary hypertension screening. The reason for screening shifted over time, from classic hypokalemia/target-organ damage toward pre-eclampsia, refractory hypertension, and hypertension in young patients.
items.caveat: Single-center, observational -- shows association with a training intervention, not a validated new screening protocol. Useful signal for your own index of suspicion, not a guideline change.
items.quiz_question: Name two of the three 'newer' indications this cohort saw driving primary aldosteronism pickups in the later period, beyond classic hypokalemia.
items.quiz_answer: Pre-eclampsia, refractory hypertension, and hypertension in young patients.

items.title: Efficacy and safety of relacorilant for the treatment of patients with Cushing's syndrome (GRACE): a multicentre, phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised-withdrawal study.
items.summary: The GRACE trial randomized adults with endogenous hypercortisolism (Cushing's syndrome with hypertension and/or hyperglycemia) who had responded to open-label relacorilant to continue the drug or switch to placebo for 12 weeks. Significantly more placebo-assigned patients lost hypertension control compared to those maintained on relacorilant (proportion difference 34%; OR 0.17, p=0.022). Notably, no cases of adrenal insufficiency, endometrial hypertrophy-associated vaginal bleeding, hypokalemia, or QT prolongation were observed, distinguishing relacorilant's safety profile from mifepristone.
items.caveat: Small randomized-withdrawal cohort (n=62 randomized); the open-label phase excluded non-responders, enriching for drug-sensitive patients and potentially overstating real-world efficacy. Study was industry-funded by Corcept Therapeutics, and primary endpoint was limited to hypertension response rather than broader remission criteria.
items.quiz_question: A 38-year-old woman with Cushing's syndrome (ectopic ACTH excluded, not a surgical candidate) achieves good blood pressure control on relacorilant during an open-label phase. Based on the GRACE trial, what is the most likely consequence of switching her to placebo at that point, and what safety concern does NOT appear to be associated with relacorilant compared to mifepristone?
items.quiz_answer: Per GRACE, she has a significantly higher risk of losing hypertension control on placebo (proportion difference 34%, p=0.022). Unlike mifepristone, relacorilant was not associated with adrenal insufficiency, endometrial hypertrophy-related vaginal bleeding, hypokalemia, or QT prolongation in this trial.

items.title: Consensus Guidelines on Inferior Petrosal Sinus Sampling: A Guideline From the Society of Vascular and Interventional Neurology Guidelines and Practice Standards Committee.
items.summary: This multidisciplinary consensus guideline standardizes the full BIPSS workflow for distinguishing Cushing's disease from ectopic ACTH secretion when biochemistry confirms ACTH-dependence but MRI is equivocal or shows a lesion under 6 mm. Key specifications include bilateral IPS catheterization with heparinization, CRH or desmopressin stimulation, a defined sampling protocol (2 pre-stimulation draws plus collections at 3, 5, 10, and 15 minutes post-stimulation), prechilled EDTA tubes with rapid ACTH processing, and prolactin measurement as an internal control. Interpretation cutoffs are IPS:peripheral ACTH ratio ≥2 pre-stimulation and ≥3 post-stimulation, with explicit guidance on recognizing false negatives.
items.caveat: Recommendations are graded by evidence level using a modified Delphi process; for many technical specifics the underlying RCT evidence is limited or absent, and much guidance is expert consensus. Institutional volume thresholds for competency are proposed but not yet validated against outcomes data.
items.quiz_question: You are evaluating a patient with biochemically confirmed ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome whose pituitary MRI shows a 4 mm equivocal lesion. You proceed to BIPSS. What stimulation agent is acceptable per the new SVIN guideline, what is the post-stimulation IPS:peripheral ACTH ratio cutoff for confirming pituitary origin, and why should prolactin be measured simultaneously?
items.quiz_answer: Either CRH or desmopressin is acceptable for stimulation. A post-stimulation IPS:peripheral ACTH ratio ≥3 confirms pituitary origin. Simultaneous prolactin measurement serves as an internal control to confirm that the IPS catheter is actually sampling venous effluent from the pituitary (adequate venous drainage), helping to identify potential false negatives due to inadequate catheter positioning.

items.title: Plasma ACTH Precursors measured by Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) ELISA as a Predictor of Silent Corticotroph Adenomas.
items.summary: In a prospective observational cohort of 264 clinically non-functioning pituitary adenomas (CNFPAs), plasma POMC measured by a 2-site ELISA (detecting POMC and pro-ACTH but not mature ACTH) was markedly higher in silent corticotroph adenomas (SCAs) than in non-SCA tumors (median 73 vs. 14 fmol/mL, p<0.001). Elevated POMC (≥39 fmol/mL) identified SCA with 85.7% sensitivity and 97.9% specificity among CNFPAs. All known SCAs with visible residual tumor had elevated POMC, suggesting potential utility for post-surgical monitoring.
items.caveat: Surgically confirmed SCA subgroup was small (n=7 in the primary analysis), limiting the precision of sensitivity/specificity estimates. The POMC ELISA used is not commercially available in most centers. External validation in independent cohorts is required before clinical adoption.
items.quiz_question: A 55-year-old man has a 2 cm clinically non-functioning pituitary adenoma. Preoperative plasma POMC level returns at 95 fmol/mL (normal <39 fmol/mL). Based on this study, what does this finding suggest about the likely tumor subtype, and what pathophysiological mechanism underlies the elevated POMC?
items.quiz_answer: An elevated plasma POMC strongly suggests the tumor is a silent corticotroph adenoma (SCA). The underlying mechanism is defective post-translational processing of POMC — the tumor produces POMC and pro-ACTH but fails to cleave them into biologically active ACTH, explaining why these patients lack overt hypercortisolism despite harboring a corticotroph-lineage tumor.
